extracted.intended_audience: general public / readers of Wikipedia interested in Donald Trump, his tweets, and related legal/policy consequences
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizing and documenting controversial public tweets by a sitting or former president, including factual context, reactions, legal implications, and platform moderation actions. The page compiles incidents, responses, and downstream effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twitter civic-integrity / violent-incitement moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter enforces a 'civic integrity' policy and has taken actions (locks, suspensions) against accounts for "repeated and severe violations" and content judged "likely to inspire others to replicate the violent acts"; Twitter also required deletion of specific tweets as a precondition for unlocking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: after the January 6 Capitol attack Twitter indefinitely locked and later permanently suspended @realDonaldTrump, citing repeated/severe violations and likelihood of inspiring violence. The page notes Twitter's 'civic integrity' policy (created 2018, expanded May 2020) as the basis for scrutiny of statements that may affect participation in democracy. Practical implication: platform moderation can restrict posting where content threatens civic processes or public safety; deletion of specified tweets can be a remediation condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform enforcement against health misinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Social platforms apply misinformation policies to public-health claims; tweets that undermine public-health messaging (e.g., downplaying COVID-19, false comparisons with flu) may be labeled or removed under platform rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Twitter placed a warning message over a tweet falsely claiming seasonal flu was more lethal than COVID-19; Facebook deleted similar posts per its policies. The page documents expert criticism that such presidential tweets 'undermined public health messaging' and encouraged disregard of public-health recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential Records Act — archiving and deletion prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: The National Archives and Records Administration recommends archiving all presidential social media postings to comply with the Presidential Records Act; deletion of public posts may constitute unlawful destruction of presidential records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: watchdog groups (CREW and the National Security Archive) sued, contending deletion of tweets violated the PRA. The practical standard: executive social-media output should be preserved as official records; deleting such posts can create legal challenges alleging record destruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blocking users and the public-forum / viewpoint-discrimination doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: When a public official uses a social-media account to conduct official business, blocking users from that account can constitute viewpoint discrimination in a public forum and thus violate the First Amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a U.S. District Court ruled that @realDonaldTrump blocked users due to viewpoint discrimination and ordered unblockings; the Second Circuit later upheld the ruling. The page notes continued litigation (petition to the Supreme Court). Practical implication: public officials should not block constituents on accounts used for official communications, or they risk constitutional challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of public social-media statements as admissible evidence of motive/intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may cite a public official's tweets and statements as evidentiary background relevant to assessing motivations, intent, or discriminatory animus behind policies and actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: federal appeals courts cited the President's tweets in assessing motive in travel-ban litigation (Fourth and Ninth Circuits); the D.C. district court in Jane Doe v. Trump relied on a tweet to support finding a lack of formal process in a policy announcement. Practical implication: public statements on social media can be relied upon by litigants and courts to infer state of mind and purpose, affecting constitutional review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright/licensing requirement for campaign media
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of copyrighted music or other media in campaign or promotional videos requires appropriate licensing; use without permission can prompt cease-and-desist and platform removal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Linkin Park issued a cease-and-desist after an unlicensed song appeared in a campaign video retweeted by Trump; Twitter disabled the video. Practical implication: campaigns and public accounts must secure licenses for third-party content or risk takedown and legal challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional/procedural limits on altering election timing
rubrics_metrics.description: The President lacks unilateral authority to change the date of federal elections; only Congress can change the date established by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: when Trump suggested delaying the 2020 election due to mail-in ballots, leaders across the spectrum noted that the President did not have the power to delay elections and only Congress could change the date. Practical implication: public calls to alter election mechanics must respect statutory/constitutional allocation of powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal/political consequences of incendiary rhetoric (threats, calls to violence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public statements by an official that appear to threaten violence (e.g., warning of 'Civil War like fracture' if removed from office) or exhort retribution can prompt calls for suspension/impeachment and may be taken seriously by violent actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a quoted remark about 'Civil War' drew criticism and legal commentary suggesting it could constitute an independent ground for impeachment; scholars warned that militia groups might take such tweets seriously. Practical implication: incendiary rhetoric from officials can produce serious legal and public-safety consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: False attribution of foreignness / xenophobic language as a basis for condemnation
rubrics_metrics.description: Tweets that falsely characterize native or naturalized citizens as foreign ('go back' tropes) are treated as xenophobic/racist and draw formal condemnations and political rebuke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Trump's 'go back' tweet aimed at four congresswomen was widely described as racist and as an example of false attribution of foreignness, prompting a House resolution condemning the comments. Practical implication: such language is evaluated as discriminatory and can generate cross-party condemnation and reputational/legal fallout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attacks on the judiciary and public confidence concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Public attacks by an official on judges and the judicial system (e.g., calling a judge 'so-called') raise concerns about undermining public confidence in the judiciary and may be highlighted by legal experts as problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Trump's tweets attacking Judge James Robart and other judicial figures prompted commentary from legal scholars warning that such comments could undermine an institution charged with checking executive power. Practical implication: disparaging judicial officials in public statements can have implications for institutional legitimacy and may be cited in legal analysis.
